content: Carrion's disease, also known as Oroya fever, is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bartonella bacilliformis. The disease is named after Daniel Alcides Carrión, a Peruvian medical student who, in 1885, self-inoculated with material from a verruga lesion of a chronic patient to study the disease. He subsequently developed the acute phase of the illness, confirming the shared etiology of the acute and chronic forms of the disease. Tragically, Carrión succumbed to bartonellosis on October 5, 1885, and is honored as a martyr of Peruvian medicine. October 5 is celebrated as Peruvian Medicine Day in his memory. The disease has been recognized since pre-Inca times, with artistic depictions of its chronic phase found in endemic areas. During the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire, chronic cases with wart-like lesions were described in Spanish troops. Historically, it was believed to be endemic only to Peru and limited to a single phase, referred to as Peruvian wart or verruga peruana. However, an outbreak in 1875 during the construction of the Lima-Oroya railroad revealed the acute phase, characterized by fever and anemia, which became known as Oroya fever. In 1905, Peruvian microbiologist Alberto Barton identified Bartonella bacilliformis within red blood cells, and in 1909, he announced it as the causative agent of the disease. Causes Carrion's disease is caused by infection with the bacterium Bartonella bacilliformis. The bacterium is transmitted to humans through the bite of sandflies belonging to the genus Lutzomyia. Epidemiology The disease is endemic to certain regions of Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia. It is particularly prevalent in specific areas of Peru. Clinical Presentation Carrion's disease has two distinct clinical phases, corresponding to the two types of host cells invaded by the bacterium: red blood cells and endothelial cells. Some individuals in endemic areas may remain asymptomatic. 1. Acute Phase (Oroya fever): Common symptoms include sustained fever (typically not exceeding 102°F or 39°C) and malaise. This phase is marked by severe hemolytic anemia and transient immunosuppression. Untreated cases have a fatality rate exceeding 40%, which can rise to 90% in the presence of opportunistic infections, such as those caused by Salmonella species. 2. Chronic Phase (Verruga peruana or Peruvian wart): This phase is characterized by an eruptive cutaneous rash due to endothelial cell proliferation, forming lesions known as Peruvian warts. Common findings include bleeding from the verrugas, fever, malaise, arthralgias, anorexia, and myalgias. Physical Examination Skin: Pallor, jaundice, and rash. Lesions can be classified into three types based on size and characteristics: Miliary (1–4 mm): Most common. Nodular or subdermic. Mular (>5 mm). Eyes: Pallor and jaundice. Neck: Lymphadenopathy. Abdomen: Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Laboratory Diagnosis Acute Phase: Diagnosis can be made using a peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa, Columbia blood agar cultures, immunoblot, indirect immunofluorescence (IFI), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Chronic Phase: Diagnosis involves Warthin-Starry staining of wart biopsy specimens, PCR, and immunoblot. Treatment 1. Acute Phase: The treatment of choice in adults is quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) or chloramphenicol. In children, chloramphenicol combined with beta-lactams is recommended. A preferred regimen includes ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. 2. Chronic Phase: Rifampin or macrolides are used to treat both adults and children.
